speaker: Boris Cherny
title: Head of Claude Code: What happens after coding is solved | Boris Cherny
question: As AI coding models rapidly improve, why do experienced engineers who have used them for a long time often underuse new capabilities compared to newcomers?
guest: One downside on a personal level is the model changes so often that I sometimes get stuck in an old way of thinking about it. I even find that new people on the team or new grads do stuff in a more forward way than I do. For example, a couple months ago there was a memory leak where memory usage kept going up until it crashed. Traditionally, you take a heap snapshot, put it into a special debugger, and look through traces to figure out what's going on. I was doing that manually, and a newer engineer on the team just had Claude Code do it—he asked it to figure out the leak. Claude Code took the heap snapshot, wrote a little just-in-time tool to analyze it itself, found the issue, and put up a pull request faster than I could. For those of us who have used the model for a long time, you have to transport yourself to the current moment and not get stuck back in an old model.

points.core: Rapid model progress leaves veterans mentally anchored to older capability limits.
points.note: Accept: Long-time users retain outdated mental models of what earlier, weaker models could not do, failing to recalibrate to new releases. Do not credit: Generic claims that senior engineers are stubborn or resistant to AI in general.

points.note: Accept: Deep muscle memory with traditional tools (e.g., manual profiling, debuggers, trace inspection) causes veterans to take over hard tasks manually instead of testing delegation. Do not credit: Surface mentions of 'habits' without connecting to manual engineering workflows.

points.core: Newcomers without legacy assumptions delegate entire open-ended problems directly to agents.
points.note: Accept: Newer engineers or recent grads lack priors about past model failures, so they hand off full multi-step problems (like building ad-hoc analysis scripts and shipping fixes) to the agent first. Do not credit: Generic praise of junior engineers being more tech-savvy or open-minded.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Mostly because their intuitions were calibrated on weaker models and never got updated. Experienced users learned, through real failures, what the tools couldn't do: they hallucinated APIs, lost track in large codebases, and broke down on multi-step tasks. So they built protective habits, such as breaking work into tiny pieces, over-specifying prompts, reviewing every line, and never delegating anything ambiguous or long-running. Those habits were rational at the time, but they persist as a fixed mental model after the limitations that justified them have disappeared.

Several things reinforce this. A task that failed once gets filed as "AI can't do that" and is rarely retried, so the belief is never tested against newer models. Established workflows still work acceptably, so there is little pressure to experiment. And expertise itself makes doing it by hand feel faster and safer than risking a delegation.

Newcomers have no such scar tissue. They simply ask for the ambitious thing, such as a whole feature, a large refactor, or an autonomous debugging session, and discover that it often works.

The remedy is to periodically retry tasks you previously wrote off, especially after each major model release.

models.label: Gemini 4 Carbon
models.answer:
Long-time AI users often operate with outdated mental models calibrated on earlier, weaker generations. Having been burned when older assistants hallucinated APIs or failed at multi-file reasoning, veterans learned which tasks were unsafe to delegate and built defensive habits, such as tightly scoped prompts and heavy micromanagement, around those historical limits. Because major capability jumps often arrive behind unchanged interfaces without signaling which former failure modes have vanished, experienced users rarely retest boundaries they wrote off months or years ago.

Deep engineering expertise compounds this inertia. Senior developers already possess fast, reliable workflows and strict standards for maintainability and verification, making open-ended delegation feel slower and riskier than sticking to proven routines—especially under delivery pressure, where reviewing subtle AI mistakes can feel costlier than writing code directly.

Newcomers arrive without this scar tissue or legacy muscle memory. Unaware of what models supposedly cannot do, they naively hand off ambitious, end-to-end work like autonomous debugging, codebase exploration, or large refactors, immediately discovering capabilities where frontier models have quietly crossed the reliability threshold.

noweb.answer: Long-time AI users carry outdated mental models shaped by earlier, weaker generations of tools. Having been burned in the past by hallucinations, small context windows, and brittle reasoning, experienced adopters built defensive habits to stay productive, such as spoon-feeding isolated snippets, micro-managing prompts, and treating AI as smart autocomplete rather than an autonomous agent. Once an engineer writes off a class of work—like multi-file refactoring, tool-driven investigation, or end-to-end debugging—they stop attempting to delegate it and therefore never see that newer models have quietly crossed that capability threshold. Because their narrow workflows still yield reliable gains, and because seasoned engineers can quickly write the hard parts themselves rather than risk troubleshooting a failed prompt, nothing forces them to re-test old assumptions. Newcomers arrive without this scar tissue or entrenched muscle memory. Unaware of historical ceilings, they hand the model ambitious, open-ended problems from day one and immediately discover its expanded reach, calibrating their habits to what today's models can actually do rather than what yesterday's could not.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
Experienced users tend to underuse new capabilities because they carry an outdated picture of what the model can do. Over months of use they learned its limits: it lost context on large codebases, broke multi-file refactors, made up APIs, and needed tight supervision. To cope, they built habits like splitting work into tiny steps, writing the hard parts themselves, giving very detailed instructions, and checking every line. Those habits made sense when they formed, but they stick around after newer models have fixed the problems behind them. The model improves in jumps, and people's expectations don't get updated the same way.

Newcomers have no record of past failures. They simply ask for the whole feature, the large refactor, or the long autonomous task, and they often find that it works. Veterans also stop trying things that failed before, so they rarely notice when something that used to fail now succeeds.

People who build these tools have made this point publicly. The practical fix is to retest your assumptions with each new model release. Hand it tasks you think are too ambitious and see what happens, rather than assuming last year's limits still hold.

models.label: Gemini 4 Neon
models.answer:
Experienced users of AI coding tools often carry outdated mental models shaped by earlier, less capable generations. Having been burned by hallucinations, broken refactors, and brittle multi-file edits, they internalize defensive habits—restricting models to narrow autocomplete, boilerplate, or heavily scaffolded prompts. Because those workflows still feel productive, there is little friction pushing veterans to re-test old boundaries, and their muscle memory quietly lags behind the frontier. Like negative transfer or learned helplessness, past failures teach you where not to look, even after the underlying limitations disappear.

Newcomers arrive without that scar tissue. Unburdened by memories of what failed a year ago, they take current capabilities at face value and readily ask models to plan architectures, debug across repositories, or run end-to-end agentic loops. Ironically, their lack of calibrated skepticism lets them discover what now works, whereas seasoned users keep optimizing for the constraints of yesterday's models until they deliberately recalibrate.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
Experienced users learned what to delegate when coding models were weaker. If broad requests often produced broken code or created more review work than they saved, engineers adapted by keeping tasks small and handling integration themselves. Those habits can outlast the limitations that made them useful.

The effect reinforces itself. If you only ask a model to write a function, you rarely get evidence that it can now trace a bug across a repository, make the fix, and run the relevant tests. A newcomer is more likely to try that whole task because they have fewer memories of similar attempts failing. The experienced engineer’s judgment was earned through real failures. models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra
models.answer:
Experienced engineers often know an earlier version of the model very well. They remember which tasks went wrong and how long the cleanup took, so they’ve learned when to take over. Those habits can outlast the limitations that made them sensible. An engineer who once had to break every feature into small edits may keep doing so and never see whether the model can now handle a whole feature.

Newcomers have fewer assumptions about where the model will fail, so they’re more likely to try a broad request and discover what it can do today. That can give them an edge in discovering capabilities, even when experienced engineers are better at judging the result.
